extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research administrators, science journalists, and readers interested in research integrity/retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing an institutional/ORI finding of research misconduct (fabrication/falsification) in publications and grant applications, and describing resulting remedies and sanctions. Focus is on describing what was done, how it violates research integrity, and the administrative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsification and fabrication by data reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowingly, intentionally, or recklessly falsified and/or fabricated data ... by reusing the data, with or without manipulation, to represent unrelated experiments from different mouse models or cell lines with different treatments in three hundred eighty-four (384) figure panels in sixteen (16) grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is ORI's characterization of misconduct in this case: reusing the same data or images to represent different experiments (even if manipulated) qualifies as falsification/fabrication. The quoted language indicates the mental state (knowing, intentional, or reckless) and the mechanism (reuse/manipulation to misrepresent experimental context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relabeling or repurposing figures to misrepresent experimental results
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing figures reporting gene expression in mice and cells after drug treatments, relabeling them to say they showed the results of different experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific example of falsification in the published papers: figure panels were reused and relabeled to indicate different experiments/conditions. This practice breaches data integrity in publications and can trigger correction or other sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of fabricated data in grant applications constitutes misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant applications contained fake data (hundreds of images across 16 grant applications), and two of those grant applications were funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing falsified data in grant proposals is treated as research misconduct by oversight bodies (ORI), regardless of whether the application is funded. Funded applications that rest on falsified data can lead to administrative sanctions and recovery actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of affected publications as an agreed remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent has agreed to request corrections for the two papers identified as containing falsified data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One common administrative remedy is that authors request corrections (or retractions) for affected publications. ORI findings may include a requirement or agreement to correct the literature as part of the resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative sanctions: bans on federal funding, contracting, and service
rubrics_metrics.description: Chang agreed to a 10-year ban from all federal contracting, including grant funding, and agreed not to serve in any advisory or consulting role with the U.S. Public Health Service (which includes the NIH) for that time period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight bodies can impose career-impacting administrative sanctions such as multi-year bans on receiving federal grants, prohibition from federal contracts, and exclusion from advisory or consulting roles with public health agencies. The article notes a decade-long ban, described as more severe than ORI has typically imposed recently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and scale of misconduct are documented and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The ORI finding details the magnitude: 384 figure panels across 16 grant applications, and reuse/manipulation in 119 figure panels across two papers and 15 grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations quantify the extent of misconduct (number of affected figures, papers, grant applications), and that scope is reported publicly; scale can be relevant to the seriousness of findings and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between administrative findings (ORI) and criminal fraud standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments note that ORI cases involve administrative law with a lower standard of proof than criminal fraud, which requires specific legal elements (knowing falsification, belief by another, action in reliance, and demonstrable injury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative and sanctioning bodies like ORI operate under administrative law; criminal prosecution requires meeting additional legal elements and a higher standard of proof. This affects remedies available (administrative sanctions vs. criminal penalties).
